judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 194, which bans releasing balloons that float away. It covers a balloon filled with a gas lighter than air. A person may not release one on purpose, organize a release, or cause one. Breaking the rule carries a civil penalty of up to $250, which the Attorney General or a local attorney can sue to collect. The ban reaches balloons made of material that takes more than five minutes in air or water to break down. It does not cover a hot air balloon that is brought back down, a balloon used in government or scientific research, or a balloon released indoors. The Nevada Assembly passed it 26-15. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 241, which requires every Nevada county and city to allow apartment buildings on land zoned for business. The rule covers a multifamily housing development, or a mixed-use project that includes homes. Allowing it by right means the project does not need a special permit or a rezoning. Land zoned for industry does not count as land zoned for business. Any local rule that conflicts with the requirement is void. The Nevada Assembly passed an earlier version 28-14. The Senate later let a local government set the standards a project must meet. It also exempted airport land and the Lake Tahoe region. And it added a gift of about five acres of state land in Reno to two charities that serve people in need. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 241, which requires every Nevada county and city to allow apartment buildings on land zoned for business. judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 527, which lets school districts put cameras on school buses to catch drivers who pass a stopped bus. A district may choose to do this. Nothing in the bill makes it. A ticket goes by mail to the registered owner of the car. The owner can push back only by swearing who was driving, or that the car was stolen. A police officer has to review the images before a ticket goes out. The fine is set locally and cannot be lower than the fine for the same offense today. A camera ticket carries no license points and no suspension. Images must be destroyed within 90 days, and the fines go to the school district. The Nevada Senate passed it 15-5. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 89, which sets rules for strip searches of children held in juvenile facilities. Each facility must write and follow a policy on them. A staff member may not strip search a child unless two things are true. The staff member must reasonably suspect the child has a weapon or contraband within reach. The staff member must also have already tried every less intrusive way of finding it. Two staff must be present for the whole search, and of the same sex as the child where possible. The staff member in charge of the search must file a written report within 72 hours. The Nevada Assembly passed it 27-15. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 96, which makes bigger Nevada counties plan for extreme heat. A master plan is the long-term plan a county or city writes for how land gets used. Counties with 100,000 or more people must now include a heat plan in it. The plan must cover access to public cooling spaces, public drinking water, cooler building methods and shade over paved areas. Shade can include shade structures and street trees, with a preference for native or drought-tolerant kinds. The bill requires the plan to be written. It does not require any county to build a cooling center, install a drinking fountain or plant a tree. The rule starts in July 2026. The Nevada Assembly passed an earlier version 29-13. The Senate later moved the heat plan inside the conservation part of the master plan, and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 183, which limits how many children one child welfare caseworker can be given. A worker who handles permanency cases may not be given more than 30 children in the agency's care. Permanency work means looking after a child's health, schooling and family life. It also means finding the child a permanent home. An agency can go past 30 to keep brothers and sisters with the same worker. It can also go past 30 for up to 30 days in an emergency, under a written policy. The cap counts only children in the agency's care. Children who are only under investigation are not counted. The Nevada Assembly passed it 33-9. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 188, which requires health care to be reachable for people who do not speak English well. Hospitals, clinics and individual providers must take reasonable steps so a language barrier does not block care. Any help with language has to be free to the patient, accurate and on time. A provider may not make the patient bring their own interpreter or pay for one. It may not use a child, or an adult who is not qualified, except in a safety emergency or at the patient's own request. A qualified translator has to check a document run through translation software when the document matters to the patient's rights or health. A facility that breaks the rules can lose its license or be fined; a provider may be disciplined by its board. The Nevada Senate passed it 13-8. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 284, which stops the state using a foster child's own benefit money to pay for the child's care. Some children in state custody are owed Social Security or veterans benefits, often after a parent dies. Under the old law that money went into a trust fund and was used to repay the government for the child's care. The bill repeals that rule and requires the agency to hold the money for the child instead. The agency must check within 60 days whether a child is owed benefits, and apply for them if so. It must keep the money in an account that does not cost the child other benefits, and account for it every six months. The change starts in January 2026. The Nevada Senate passed it 14-7. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 442, which makes utilities report how often they shut off power, gas or water at homes. The Public Utilities Commission has to write rules requiring the reports. A utility must publish one every three months. The report has to give the number of shutoffs each month for the previous quarter. It must also give combined details about the households cut off, including their zip codes. The bill requires the numbers to be published. It does not itself change when a utility may shut off service. The Nevada Assembly passed it 28-14. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 76, which sets up a state fund to pay people cheated in securities fraud. Someone a court has awarded restitution can apply to the Securities Division within a year. An award cannot be more than $25,000, or a quarter of the unpaid restitution, whichever is smaller. Anyone who takes an award has to pay the state back if they later collect from the wrongdoer. The bill puts no money in the fund. It is filled only by gifts, grants, interest and those repayments, so a victim has no guarantee of being paid. The Nevada Senate passed it 13-7. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 88, which deals with medical debt people owe the prison system when they get out. Prisons in Nevada charge people for some medical care, and the bill they leave with can follow them. The version the Senate voted told the head of the Department of Corrections to wipe that debt out on release. It reached people released before July 2025 too. The Nevada Senate passed the version that wiped the debt out, 14-7. The Assembly later changed it to a ban on collecting the debt, and let collection restart if the person returns to prison, and the bill was signed into law.
